A couple preliminary findings if you are considering adopting this extension to replace your previous pgvector's HNSW indexing.

- pg_vectorsearch uses a quantized IVF index called PRISM. PRISM caps at 1968 dimensions for vectors. If your previous HNSW has more dimensions than that, you're SOL (at least for now until they fix that).

- pg_vectorsearch shipped yesterday and it's obviously alpha. Hasn't been battle tested in production environments outside of Timescale's. Also since it's so new, it isn't on Azure's allowed-extension list or any other Hyperscale's managed PG instances' allowed extension list. It takes time to graduate from alpha and mature. So if you run managaed PG instances from hyperscaler's cloud, you're SOL (at least for now until this matures into those ecosystems) or you have to migrate to a PG 18 self-hosted.

- pg_vectorsearch requires Postgres version 18 or above. If you run PG versions below that you need to migrate your database first. Many legacy PG production environment are way dated on PG 14 or 15, migration is prohibitively high cost to just try this out.

I realise now I'm arguing with people who actually know very little at all about Britain's industrial history. Britain held a comparable position to current China or the US (high tech and bulk volume) manufacturing for ~100 years despite being about 2% of the world's population (and competing with the US, Germany, France, Italy, Russia, etc).

That sounds ludicrous now - it was ludicrous then too. Yet it really happened, and it really is over.

Women (working-class women) were actually an essential part of the industrial workforce during that time and dominated some of the industries like textile manufacturing. Only as the middle class grew with prosperity did this even begin to change at all. Laws were passed to limit their working hours to 60 a week and prevent them from working in underground mining. There were many lady engineers and inventors too, beginning the in the late 19th (peak) and accelerating with early 20th (WWI).

England was famous not for 'men with hammers' but for highly skilled craftsmen, inventors, and engineers who produced the bulk of the most sophisticated manufactured goods in the world - textiles, steam engines and turbines, ocean liners, scientific instruments, mechanical and then electronic calculators, chemicals and dyes, weaponry, steel and other metals, mining and heavy industrial equipment, electric motors and generators, radios and televisions, radar, photography and cameras, engines, cars, even tyres, plastics, cement. These are all industries with the British created and dominated.
